summary: Discovery call to understand Asterion's need for reserved GPU capacity with strict tenant isolation and occasional high-volume bursts driven by nightly processing and peak clinical loads. Key concerns: encryption/KMS, audit logs, warm-pool prewarmed duration, eviction behavior during storms, and predictable latency for SLAs. Redwood AE+SE outlined Dedicated options, hybrid fallback to Hosted, and proposed a short benchmark and throughput estimate.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-13 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48 minutes | Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood Solutions), Marcus Hale (CTO, Asterion), Lina Torres (Infra), Raj Patel (SRE), Nia Owens (Product)

[00:00:00] Alex Moreno: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. um yeah we scheduled 45 minutes ish to walk through your reserved capacity needs and figure out what dedicated looks like for you. can you quick run through the big pain points?

[00:00:10] Marcus Hale: Sure — thanks Alex. So at Asterion we run clinical summarization and triage models, and we have two things: steady baseline traffic for chat notes and then these nightly batch spikes when labs and devices push results. spikes can be 60 to 120 qps for short windows, like 10-20 minutes, sometimes longer if a downstream batch retries.

[00:00:33] Lina Torres: And from infra perspective we need tenant isolation, we can't have noisy neighbor risk — PHI compliance is critical. We need to confirm encryption in transit & at rest, KMS integration, and a clear audit trail for model requests.

[00:00:45] Raj Patel: Also, eviction behavior and prewarm semantics matter. We can't have requests queued for minutes during a storm. What's Redwood's warm pool and hot node eviction policy?

[00:00:55] Alex Moreno: Great questions. Priya from our SE team will go deep on warm pool / eviction and throughput. High level: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools, and we offer hotpool prewarmed nodes plus burst capacity depending on reserved tier. We also have a fallback to hosted variants if you want seamless degradation.

[00:01:10] Priya Singh: Hi all. quick caveat, I'll try to be precise but some of the names might get fuzzy; transcription may show K V cache sometimes, apologies. On warm pool: we have a configurable warm window — you can set hot nodes to remain prewarmed for X minutes after idle. Longer prewarm increases cost. Eviction: we preferentially reclaim ephemeral capacity from lowest-priority tenants, but for Dedicated reserved pools you get tenancy guarantees within that pool; eviction only happens for overcommit scenarios or infra failures.

[00:01:40] Marcus Hale: How deterministic is latency under heavy tail? Our SLA is 300ms p95 for short responses.

[00:01:47] Priya Singh: For short responses and typical models, within a dedicated pool tuned for that model, 300ms p95 is achievable. It depends on model size, quantization, and batching window. If you use our low-latency profile — minimal batching, prewarmed kv cache — you'll hit that. Bulk/batch jobs will be different.

[00:02:05] Lina Torres: We care about KMS — we use an HSM-backed KMS. Can Redwood integrate customer-managed keys and ensure model cache artifacts aren't persisted unencrypted?

[00:02:15] Jordan Lee: Yes. Private deployments and Dedicated both support customer KMS integrations; we can map keys for audit and ensure disk encryption. For Hosted fallback, keys are managed by Redwood unless you enable the private key path on Private deployment. We'll follow up with the security whitepaper that shows the flow.

[00:02:33] Raj Patel: On multi-tenant vs dedicated: if we reserve a pool but still allow cross-tenant bursts, how does isolation work?

[00:02:39] Priya Singh: With Dedicated reserved pools you can configure tenant fencing: strict (single-tenant on GPU nodes) or soft (logical isolation with tenant quotas). Single-tenant gives the strongest isolation but costs more. Soft fencing can be fine if you have strict RBAC and network segmentation.

[00:02:56] Marcus Hale: Where does Private deployment fit? I hear Redwood Private has a control plane you manage — is that our on-prem option?

[00:03:02] Alex Moreno: Private is for VPC or on-prem: you run the inference runtime in your environment with Redwood control plane optional. That gives you full control over data flow, KMS, and audit logs. It usually requires a longer integration and separate licensing.

[00:03:12] Nia Owens: Timeline question — we're hoping to commit to reserved capacity for Q1 2027. What lead time should we expect for procurement and reserved pool provisioning?

[00:03:20] Priya Singh: Provisioning GPUs in a Dedicated pool typically takes 2–6 weeks depending on region and capacity. For Private on-prem, plan for 8–12 weeks for validated deployment. Longer if you need SOC2 ISO paperwork and legal.

[00:03:33] Lina Torres: Pricing sensitivity — when you say reserved tiers, are those monthly commitments? How flexible is bursting beyond the reserved amount?

[00:03:41] Alex Moreno: Reserved is typically monthly or annual commit. Bursting can be configured as on-demand capacity in the same region, billed at overage rates, or via a paid burst buffer. We can model a hybrid: baseline reserved + limited burst credits.

[00:03:55] Marcus Hale: Ok, specifics: imagine baseline 15 qps steady, plus 120 qps spikes for 10–20 minutes twice a day. Also, we need retention of logs for 7 years for audits. Is that doable?

[00:04:06] Jordan Lee: Log retention is configurable but 7 years is enterprise-level — we can retain logs in your S3 or your storage if Private; Hosted can support long-term retention with add-on pricing. We'll include retention options in the follow-up doc.

[00:04:18] Raj Patel: Benchmarking — we want to run a smoke benchmark before signing. Could we do a 30 minute run that simulates spikes and check p95/p99 and cost estimates?

[00:04:26] Priya Singh: Yes, we do a short benchmark in staging Dedicated. For the 120 qps spike, we'll need to know average tokens per request and model variant. Do you use a 70B or 13B family?

[00:04:36] Marcus Hale: We're on 13B-ish models for now. typical completion length is 120 tokens, prompts 60 tokens. So 180 tokens per request average.

[00:04:44] Priya Singh: Great — that helps. Quick back-of-the-envelope: 120 qps * 180 tokens ~= 21,600 tokens/s. For a 13B quantized profile, that's heavy but doable with a hotpool of multiple GPUs. We'll run more precise numbers and include batching strategy — aggressive batching reduces cost but hurts latency, so we'll profile both.

[00:05:05] Lina Torres: About burst strategy — if we prewarm say 4 GPUs in hotpool, what's the idle cost? Do you charge per-minute?

[00:05:12] Alex Moreno: Billing is per minute at the node level for prewarmed capacity in most plans; you can choose reserved v. hotpool retained minutes. We'll put exact pricing in the doc — we can also model a 'spare capacity' buffer to absorb short storms.

[00:05:24] Raj Patel: Eviction detail — what happens if the physical host needs maintenance and we have prewarmed nodes reclaimed? Is there an automatic failover to hosted fallback?

[00:05:32] Priya Singh: For Dedicated we can configure automatic fallback policies: fallback to a compatible hosted model variant in another region or a lower-cost quantized variant. That reduces overall availability risk. In Private on-prem we'd recommend a multi-zone setup and a warm standby.

[00:05:47] Marcus Hale: Are there hard limits on model size or kv-cache persistence with Dedicated? We use KV caching extensively for chat continuity.

[00:05:55] Priya Singh: No hard model size limits beyond hardware capability. KV cache is supported; in Dedicated we keep KV in-memory on the node; if you need cross-node stickiness we can do sticky routing or prefix cache replication but that increases complexity. We'll describe tradeoffs.

[00:06:10] Jordan Lee: small note — sometimes the transcriptions call KV 'K V', just so you know if the doc looks odd.

[00:06:15] Nia Owens: On compliance side — do you have SOC2 Type II, and can you provide penetration test reports?

[00:06:20] Alex Moreno: Yes, Redwood has SOC2 Type II. We can share redacted pen test summaries under NDA. For Private deployments we support stronger attestations and can run joint penetration exercises.

[00:06:29] Marcus Hale: Okay, sounds good. One more thing: data residency. We host in us-east now but require EU storage for EEA patients. Can dedicated pools be region-restricted?

[00:06:37] Priya Singh: Absolutely — pools are regionally pinned. For multiregion needs we can set geo-routing and a policy that keeps EU data in EU regions only.

[00:06:46] Raj Patel: Any gotchas around autoscaling during spikes? For example, if we rely on autoscale and it takes 3 minutes to spin GPUs, we could miss SLAs.

[00:06:54] Priya Singh: That's why hotpool prewarm is recommended for short spikes. Autoscale handles longer growth but has cold-starts. You can set prewarm heuristics, keep minimal hot nodes for SLA, and allow autoscale for sustained increases. We'll show simulation curves.

[00:07:10] Marcus Hale: How does the trial/benchmark work contractually? If we run the 30-minute benchmark and it's good, does that convert to a credit?

[00:07:17] Alex Moreno: We typically offer benchmark credits or discounted pilot tiers; conversion to committed reserved billing is a commercial discussion. We'll outline standard pilot terms in the follow-up.

[00:07:26] Speaker 1 (unlabeled): Can you share a sample SLA or an SLO table?

[00:07:30] Alex Moreno: Yes — we'll attach an SLO table that maps to reserved tiers: latency p95, availability, mean time to fallback, etc.

[00:07:36] Priya Singh: For the action items — I'll start the throughput calc with their numbers (13B, 180 tokens/request, 120 qps spikes) and produce two profiles: latency-optimized and cost-optimized.

[00:07:45] Marcus Hale: Perfect. For decision criteria we need: cost per qps, predictable p95, KMS integration, and log retention cost. If you can present those side-by-side it's easiest.

[00:07:55] Alex Moreno: We'll do that. Anything else on compliance or security?

[00:08:00] Lina Torres: Please include details on network egress, VPC peering setup, and whether we can push logs to our SIEM.

[00:08:07] Jordan Lee: Yes to all — SIEM forwarding supported, VPC peering for Private, and dedicated private link options for Hosted/Dedicated. We'll show diagrams.

[00:08:15] Nia Owens: timeline recap: we'll get the pricing and pilot plan by 10/15, throughput calc by 10/20, we'll aim to run the benchmark week of 10/25, and decision by end of November.

[00:08:26] Alex Moreno: That matches our notes. Any final questions?

[00:08:29] Marcus Hale: Not from me. thanks everyone, looking forward.

[00:08:33] Alex Moreno: Great — we'll follow up with the docs and set the benchmark slot. Thanks all.

[00:08:40] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: medium — some speaker labels generic, few mis-transcriptions for acronyms (KV -> K V), occasional run-on sentences.
